runs.text: One Israeli snack. Ten times fewer peanut allergies? Tel Aviv. A London allergist, Gideon Lack, gives a lecture. Very few doctors there have ever seen a child with peanut allergy. Why? Israeli babies eat Bamba in their first year. Puffed corn, coated in peanut butter. Bamba launched in nineteen sixty four as a cheese snack. It flopped. Peanut butter saved it. So his team compared Jewish children in Britain and Israel. Same heritage, different snack. In Britain, one point eight five percent had a peanut allergy. In Israel, zero point one seven percent. About ten times fewer. Then came a real trial, called LEAP: high risk babies, fed peanut from infancy to age five. The result: up to eighty one percent fewer peanut allergies. In twenty seventeen, America flipped its advice. Peanut early, not late. In twenty twenty four, the trial kids were teenagers. Still protected. Bamba isn't medicine.
